text: forge coverage compiles your project for source mapping, runs your test suite, and reports which lines, statements, branches, and functions were actually executed by at least one test. Running it with a summary report shows you percentages per file.

For CI integration or an external dashboard like Codecov or Coveralls, you generate an LCOV tracefile instead, with forge coverage --report lcov. That's the format most coverage tools and CI dashboards actually consume.

Coverage answers exactly one question: did any test execute this line? It says nothing about whether the test that executed it actually asserted the right thing. A test that calls withdraw and asserts nothing at all still counts as covering every line inside withdraw. Coverage measures that code ran, not that it was checked.

That gap is exactly why this chapter built fuzz testing and invariant testing as separate disciplines, not as a coverage number to chase. Branch coverage at 100% doesn't mean every combination of branches across a call sequence was tested — that's invariant testing. Line coverage at 100% doesn't mean boundary values were exercised at each line — that's fuzz testing. Function coverage at 100% just means every function was called once; it says nothing about whether it was called from an unauthorized address.

Use coverage as a map of blind spots, not a target. A function at zero percent is one nobody has thought about testing at all — that's actionable. A function at 100% tells you nothing about whether the assertions inside those tests are strong. Treat a coverage percentage as the start of a review, not the end of one. You're ready for Chapter 2 once you can explain why a function can sit at 100% line coverage and still contain an untested, exploitable bug.
